growth_story.headline: Argentina's income per person grew in the 1990s and 2000s booms, then stalled after 2013; it is still 5.4 percent below its 2011 peak.
growth_story.arc: From 1990 to 1997 income per person grew 3.5 percent a year, and from 1991 the peso was pegged to the US dollar. From 1998 to 2005 growth slowed to 0.3 percent a year: income per person fell each year from 1999 to 2002, by 11.8 percent in 2002, as rising public debt ended in a default in December 2001 and the end of the peg, before a fast rebound. From 2006 to 2013 growth ran at 3.0 percent a year during the 2000s commodity boom, and income per person peaked in 2011. Since 2014 it has averaged -0.3 percent a year; the IMF links the slide to falling productivity under distortive policies, heavy state intervention and controls, while deficits paid for with printed money, the 2020 pandemic and a drought in 2023 added shocks. A stabilization drive that began at the end of 2023 brought a rebound of 4.0 percent in 2025, but income per person is still 5.4 percent below its 2011 peak and about where it first was in 2008.

threads.title: Pegged peso, then default
threads.text: From 1991 the peso was tied one-for-one to the US dollar, and growth was strong until 1997. Public debt rose steadily, and the slump that followed ended in a sovereign default in December 2001 and the end of the peg. Income per person fell 11.8 percent in 2002.

threads.title: Boom gains, then lost ground
threads.text: The 2000s commodity boom lifted income per person to a peak in 2011. The IMF says those gains were then reversed, and ties the decline to falling productivity under distortive policies, state intervention and heavy controls that held back private investment and formal jobs.

citations.quote: falling productivity, stemming from distortive policies, extensive state intervention, and burdensome regulations and controls that discouraged private investment and formal employment

threads.title: Deficits paid with printed money
threads.text: The IMF describes a long record of the central bank paying for government deficits, which fed high inflation and repeated booms and busts. From 2020 to 2023 this pushed inflation to triple digits despite price controls, on top of the shock of the global pandemic, in which income per person fell 10.3 percent in 2020.

citations.title: Argentina: Request for an Extended Arrangement Under the Extended Fund Facility-Press Release; Staff Report; Staff Supplement; and Statement by the Executive Director for Argentina

threads.title: Stabilization and its strains
threads.text: Since 2024 the government has run budget surpluses and stopped the central bank from paying for the government. Income per person fell in 2023 and 2024, then grew 4.0 percent in 2025, though political uncertainty before the October 2025 midterm elections set off a rush into dollars and slowed growth for a time.

threads.title: Farms, energy and mining lead
threads.text: A drought hit farm output in 2023, and farming recovered the next year. Growth now leans on agribusiness, energy and mining, and Argentina has become a net energy exporter, but these sectors create few jobs for their size while manufacturing and construction lag.

growth_story.tension: The IMF describes a deep fall in income per person after 2011, while in this tool's data the fall is shallower: even before the 2025 rebound the drop from the 2011 peak is smaller than the IMF's figure, and by 2025 income per person is only 5.4 percent below that peak, so the tool reads the shortfall as context rather than the growth problem.
